pieces.h: Voltage, current, resistance: the three numbers
pieces.d: Every circuit you will ever meet is a story about three quantities. Learn what each one is and the rest of electronics stops being magic.

pieces.h: Sleep: what it is doing while you are out
pieces.d: You spend a third of your life asleep, and it is not downtime. Knowing the machinery makes the standard advice easier to follow.

pieces.h: How a habit actually forms
pieces.d: A habit is a behaviour your brain has stopped deciding about. Understanding the loop behind it tells you where to push if you want to build one or break one.

pieces.h: Compound interest: the curve that bends
pieces.d: Growth on top of growth looks like nothing for years and then looks like magic. The arithmetic is simple, and time is the ingredient you cannot buy later.

pieces.h: Pot odds: the price of a call
pieces.d: Every call is a purchase. Pot odds tell you the price, and whether the hand you hold is worth paying it.

pieces.h: The printing press: when copies became cheap
pieces.d: Around 1450 a goldsmith in Mainz found a way to mass-produce the written word. Within two generations, Europe was a different place.

pieces.h: Ohm's law in your head
pieces.d: One short formula does most of the arithmetic in electronics. Here is how to use it without a calculator and how to know when it stops applying.

pieces.h: Strength training: the short version
pieces.d: Lifting heavy things on purpose is among the best-supported habits for a long and capable life. The principles fit on one page.

pieces.h: If-then plans: the smallest trick that works
pieces.d: Good intentions fail at a predictable point: the moment of action. One sentence, written in advance, moves the decision out of that moment.

pieces.h: Index funds: buying the whole haystack
pieces.d: Instead of hunting for the winning stocks, own all of them. It sounds like giving up. Over long periods it has beaten most of the professionals.

pieces.h: Outs and the rule of 2 and 4
pieces.d: Count the cards that save you, multiply by two or by four, and you have your chance of improving, close enough to act on.

pieces.h: Germ theory: the invisible cause
pieces.d: For most of history, nobody knew what made people sick. The discovery that tiny living things cause disease is barely 150 years old.

pieces.h: Power and heat: why parts burn
pieces.d: Voltage and current together make power, and power that has nowhere to go becomes heat. This is the sum that decides whether a part survives.

pieces.h: Cardio: how much, how hard
pieces.d: Your heart and lungs adapt to what you ask of them. The guidelines are modest, the benefits are large, and most of the work should feel easy.

pieces.h: Attention is the scarce thing
pieces.d: You cannot do two demanding things at once, and switching between them costs more than it feels like. Protecting attention is mostly a matter of design.

pieces.h: Risk, volatility and why diversification works
pieces.d: Spreading money around is the one move in investing that lowers risk without necessarily lowering return. Here is the mechanism behind the slogan.

pieces.h: Equity: your share of the pot
pieces.d: Before the last card is dealt, nobody owns the pot. Equity is the share that belongs to you on average, and thinking in shares changes how you play.

pieces.h: Plate tectonics: the ground is moving
pieces.d: The continents drift at the speed your fingernails grow. The idea was ridiculed for half a century before the evidence from the sea floor settled it.

pieces.h: Series and parallel: two ways to connect anything
pieces.d: There are only two basic ways to join parts. Knowing which one you are looking at tells you what the voltage and current must be doing.

pieces.h: Protein: how much you need and why
pieces.d: Protein is the one nutrient your body cannot store for later. The basics of how much, when and from what are simpler than the supplement aisle suggests.

pieces.h: Spaced repetition: remembering on purpose
pieces.d: Forgetting follows a curve. Review something just as it is about to slip and you flatten the curve, with a fraction of the effort cramming takes.

pieces.h: Inflation: the slow leak in every dollar
pieces.d: Prices rise a little each year, and a little each year becomes a lot over a working life. Understanding the leak changes how you think about saving.

pieces.h: Expected value: the only score that counts
pieces.d: Results tell you what happened. Expected value tells you whether the decision was right. Poker is won by people who learn to tell the two apart.

pieces.h: Natural selection in five minutes
pieces.d: The most important idea in biology needs only three ingredients, and none of them involves intention. Here is what it claims and what it does not.

pieces.h: The voltage divider: the most reused circuit there is
pieces.d: Two resistors and one idea. It sets reference levels, reads sensors and shrinks signals, and it hides inside thousands of larger circuits.

pieces.h: Caffeine: how the world's favourite drug works
pieces.d: Most adults take it every day. It does not give you energy. It hides the signal that you are tired, which is useful if you know the rules.

pieces.h: Test yourself: retrieval beats rereading
pieces.d: The most common study method, reading it again, is one of the weakest. Pulling information out of your head teaches you more than putting it back in.

pieces.h: The emergency fund: boring money that buys freedom
pieces.d: A few months of expenses in plain cash earns almost nothing and is still one of the best financial decisions most people can make.

pieces.h: Implied odds: the money that is not in the pot yet
pieces.d: Sometimes the price of a call is wrong on paper and right in practice, because of what you stand to win later. Here is when that is true and when it is wishful.

pieces.h: DNA: the molecule that carries instructions
pieces.d: Four chemical letters, arranged along a twisted ladder, hold the plans for every living thing. Here is how that works and how it was found.

pieces.h: AC and DC: why the wall and the battery disagree
pieces.d: Batteries push one way. The wall socket reverses direction many times a second. The reasons are historical, practical and still shaping every gadget you own.

pieces.h: Water: how much you actually need
pieces.d: Eight glasses a day is a rule nobody can trace to solid evidence. Your body already has a precise system for this, and it mostly works.

pieces.h: Procrastination is not about time
pieces.d: Putting things off looks like a planning problem. The research points somewhere else: it is a way of managing a bad feeling, and that changes the fix.

pieces.h: Getting out of debt: avalanche, snowball and the minimum trap
pieces.d: There are two well-known orders in which to pay off debts. One is cheaper. The other is easier to stick with. Both beat the default.

pieces.h: Fold equity: winning without the best hand
pieces.d: A bet can win two ways: by being called and holding up, or by making the other player fold. The second way has a value you can estimate.

pieces.h: The periodic table: a map that predicted the future
pieces.d: A Russian chemistry teacher arranged the known elements on cards and left gaps for ones nobody had found. He was right about the gaps.

pieces.h: Resistors: reading them and choosing them
pieces.d: The cheapest part on the board and the one you will use most. How to read the stripes, pick a value and avoid the three usual mistakes.

pieces.h: Knife skills: the fifteen-minute upgrade
pieces.d: One good knife, held properly and kept sharp, makes cooking faster and safer than a drawer full of gadgets.

pieces.h: Confirmation bias: the mother of all biases
pieces.d: People do not weigh evidence evenly. We look for what agrees with us, and we are far better at spotting flaws in arguments we dislike.

pieces.h: How a mortgage really works
pieces.d: The monthly payment never changes, but what it buys changes every month. Seeing the schedule explains why early extra payments are so powerful.

pieces.h: Counting combinations: how many ways can they have it
pieces.d: You cannot see their cards, but you can count how many versions of each hand exist. That count is what turns a guess into an estimate.

pieces.h: Entropy: why time has a direction
pieces.d: Eggs break and do not unbreak. Coffee cools and never reheats itself. One law of physics explains why the film of the world only runs one way.

pieces.h: Capacitors: small tanks for charge
pieces.d: A capacitor stores a little energy and gives it back quickly. That one behaviour smooths power, blocks DC, sets timing and keeps chips alive.

pieces.h: Browning: the chemistry that makes food taste good
pieces.d: The crust on a steak, the colour of toast and the smell of roasting coffee come from the same reaction. Controlling it is the core of savoury cooking.

pieces.h: Anchoring: the first number wins
pieces.d: An arbitrary figure mentioned at the start of a judgement drags the final answer toward itself, even when everyone knows it is meaningless.

pieces.h: Credit scores: what the number measures
pieces.d: A three-digit number decides what you pay to borrow. It follows a small set of rules, and most of them reward doing boring things for a long time.

pieces.h: Variance and bankroll: surviving your own luck
pieces.d: A winning player can lose for weeks. Knowing how wide the swings run, and keeping enough money to ride them, is part of the skill.

pieces.h: Relativity in five minutes
pieces.d: Einstein's two theories changed what space, time and gravity mean. The core ideas can be stated without mathematics, and your phone depends on them.

pieces.h: Inductors: the part that fights change in current
pieces.d: Coil a wire and it gains inertia. Inductors make switching power supplies possible, and their kickback is why relays kill transistors.

pieces.h: Cast iron: care without the superstition
pieces.d: A cast iron pan can outlive its owner and needs less fuss than its reputation suggests. Most of the rules people repeat about it are out of date.

pieces.h: Loss aversion: why losing hurts more than winning feels good
pieces.d: The pain of losing a sum is felt more sharply than the pleasure of gaining the same sum. That imbalance bends decisions about money, work and risk.

pieces.h: Tax brackets: why a raise never costs you money
pieces.d: A widespread fear holds that earning more can push you into a higher bracket and leave you with less. With a marginal system, that is not how it works.

pieces.h: Position: the seat is worth more than the cards
pieces.d: Acting last is the single largest structural advantage in hold'em. Good players build their whole strategy around it.

pieces.h: The double slit: the experiment that breaks intuition
pieces.d: Send particles one at a time through two openings and they build a pattern only waves can make. Check which opening each used and the pattern vanishes.

pieces.h: Diodes: the one-way valve
pieces.d: A diode lets current through in one direction and blocks it in the other. That simple trick protects, rectifies, regulates and makes light.

pieces.h: Cooking temperatures: the numbers that keep you safe
pieces.d: Colour and time are unreliable guides to whether food is safe. A cheap thermometer and four numbers remove the guesswork.

pieces.h: The availability heuristic: vivid is not the same as likely
pieces.d: We judge how common something is by how easily examples come to mind. That shortcut serves us well until memory is fed a distorted sample.

pieces.h: Reading an income statement
pieces.d: A company's income statement tells the story of a year in a dozen lines. Read from the top down, it shows where the money came from and where each slice went.

pieces.h: Starting hands: what you are really choosing
pieces.d: Choosing which hands to play is the first decision and the most frequent. The right answer depends on what kind of hand it is, not just how pretty it looks.

pieces.h: How GPS knows where you are
pieces.d: Your phone finds its position by listening to clocks in orbit. It never sends a signal, and the method depends on timing to billionths of a second.

pieces.h: LEDs: what they need and why they die
pieces.d: An LED is easy to light and easy to kill. The difference is one resistor and an understanding of why current, not voltage, is what you control.

pieces.h: How to read a nutrition label
pieces.d: The panel on the back of the packet answers most questions about a food in under a minute, if you know which three lines to read first.

pieces.h: Base rates: start with how often it happens
pieces.d: Before judging a specific case, ask how things usually turn out for cases like it. Ignoring that step produces confident and badly wrong answers.

pieces.h: The balance sheet: what a company owns and owes
pieces.d: If the income statement is a film of the year, the balance sheet is a photograph of one day. It rests on a single equation that always holds.

pieces.h: Raise or fold: why limping loses
pieces.d: Just calling the big blind feels cheap and safe. It is the mark of a losing player, and the reasons are structural.

pieces.h: How we know the universe had a beginning
pieces.d: The claim that everything began about 13.8 billion years ago rests on three independent lines of evidence that all point the same way.

pieces.h: The transistor as a switch
pieces.d: A small current controlling a large one. This is the idea underneath every relay driver, every logic gate and every processor ever made.

pieces.h: Cleaning chemistry: what works and what must never be mixed
pieces.d: Most household cleaning comes down to four kinds of chemical. Knowing which does what saves money, and knowing what not to combine prevents real harm.

pieces.h: The pre-mortem: finding the failure before it happens
pieces.d: Imagine the project has already failed, then explain why. Ten minutes of this exercise surfaces risks that weeks of planning politely overlook.

pieces.h: Profit is not cash
pieces.d: Businesses rarely die from lack of profit. They die when the cash runs out. The difference between the two is the most practical idea in accounting.

pieces.h: The 3-bet: reraising before the flop
pieces.d: A reraise before the flop is the strongest ordinary move in the game. Used well, it wins pots immediately and sets up the rest of the hand.

pieces.h: How vaccines train the immune system
pieces.d: A vaccine is a rehearsal. It shows the body a harmless preview of a germ so that the real thing meets a prepared defence.

pieces.h: MOSFETs: switching real power with almost no effort
pieces.d: The transistor inside nearly every modern device is controlled by voltage, not current. That difference is why it runs cool while switching amps.

pieces.h: Defending the big blind
pieces.d: You have already paid for part of the pot. That discount changes which hands you should play, and misjudging it is one of the costliest leaks in the game.

pieces.h: Op-amps: two rules that explain almost everything
pieces.d: The operational amplifier is the universal building block of analog electronics. Two simple rules let you analyse most circuits built around one.

pieces.h: Stack-to-pot ratio: how deep the hand really is
pieces.d: One number, worked out on the flop, tells you how strong a hand needs to be before you are willing to play for everything.

pieces.h: The multimeter: the one tool to buy first
pieces.d: If you own a single piece of test equipment, this is it. Knowing its four main functions, and its one dangerous mistake, covers most of what you need.

pieces.h: Reading the board: wet, dry and who it favours
pieces.d: Three cards land and the hand changes character. Learning to classify a flop quickly tells you who should be betting and how much.

pieces.h: Soldering that works the first time
pieces.d: A good solder joint takes three seconds and lasts decades. A bad one looks almost the same. The difference is where you put the heat.

pieces.h: The continuation bet
pieces.d: You raised before the flop and the flop has come. Betting again is the most frequent play in poker, and knowing when not to is where the profit lies.

pieces.h: Breadboards: building without solder
pieces.d: A plastic block full of holes lets you assemble a circuit in minutes and change it in seconds. Knowing how the holes connect saves hours of confusion.

pieces.h: Bet sizing: saying it with chips
pieces.d: How much you bet is as much a part of the play as whether you bet. A few principles cover most situations.

pieces.h: How to read a schematic
pieces.d: A schematic is a map of connections, not a picture of a circuit. Once you know the conventions, any diagram becomes readable.

pieces.h: Value betting: getting paid by worse hands
pieces.d: Most of the money in poker is won by betting good hands and being called by slightly worse ones. Missing those bets is an invisible leak.
